newsitem.title: IRAQ: Turkish troops chase rebel Kurds in northern Iraq.
newsitem.headline: Turkish troops chase rebel Kurds in northern Iraq.

text.p: Heavily-armed Turkish troops, backed by air, pursued separatist Kurds in northern Iraq on Thursday, the second day of their joint move with an Iraqi Kurd group to crush the guerrillas.
Thousands of troops, backed by tanks, artillery and air power, moved in before dawn on Wednesday and drove rebel Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK) units toward Iraqi government lines well to the south.
Turkish F-16 jets flew bombing missions from various air bases in southeast Turkey overnight on Wednesday, but there was no action as of early Thursday, according to reports from the remote region.

Residents in the Turkish town of Cizre, 45 km (30 miles) from the Iraqi border, said the route towards northern Iraq was quiet on Thursday morning. Dozens of troops, tanks and artillery had continued filing along the road to Iraq through Wednesday.
But security in the town, always high, remained tighter than ever, residents said.
Defence Minister Turhan Tayan said the Iraq operation -- the biggest since a 35,000-man, six-week incursion in 1995 -- was a "humanitarian mission" to protect Iraqi Kurds from the PKK.
"The troops will withdraw when the operation is over," he told reporters. Turkish army officers in Iraq were tight-lipped.
A Turkish official at the main Habur border crossing said around 10,000 troops had crossed over from the area.
Residents said the troops were supported by up to 100 tanks and armoured personnel carriers. U.S.-made Cobra helicopters provided air support.
Baghdad demanded an immediate withdrawal, saying the incursion breached international law. It said there were many casualties.

The Turkish assault followed a security sweep by local Kurdish authorities, who ordered all journalists to leave the area around Zakho, the main Iraqi border town. The border was sealed to civilian traffic.

A Western photographer who provides pictures for Reuters said his film was confiscated and he was expelled from Zakho shortly before the operation began. Local officials told him they had been ordered to impose a "news blackout".

Turkish officials said on Thursday that the blackout still held, and civilians were barred from crossing over the Habur border gate into northern Iraq. Police prevented reporters from moving beyond Cizre.

The anti-Baghdad Iraqi National Congress, citing what it said were satellite telephone contacts inside Iraq, said Turkish forces had cut the road between Dohuk, one of the main cities of the Kurdish north, and the Baghdad-controlled city of Mosul.

PKK fighters had fallen back under the assault, with some forced to flee the "safe haven," carved out by Western forces to protect the Kurds after the Gulf war, for the safety of government territory. Others moved east toward Iran.

With reporters barred from the immediate area by gunmen of the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) -- the region's leading Iraqi Kurdish faction and a strong PKK rival -- it was impossible to confirm the scope of the Turkish thrust.
A Turkish Foreign Ministry spokesman said the operation was a "limited" one, at the invitation of the Iraqi Kurds, to expel PKK guerrillas from bases along the border.
However, a senior security source told Reuters: "This is a wide and comprehensive operation."
